titleEn: Poly-B Pipe Replacement in Vancouver: Costs, Process and What to Know Before You Renovate
titleZh: 温哥华Poly-B水管更换：费用、流程及装修前必知事项
contentEn:
If you own a Vancouver-area home built between approximately 1975 and 2000, there is a roughly 40% chance your house has Poly-B piping — a grey plastic plumbing system that was installed in millions of Canadian homes before it was definitively linked to premature failures, class-action lawsuits, and insurance refusals. Reno Stars has completed seven Poly-B replacement projects in Metro Vancouver since 2022, ranging from a partial repipe in a Coquitlam townhouse to a full re-pipe of a 1991 Richmond detached home.

What Is Poly-B Pipe

Polybutylene (Poly-B) is a flexible grey plastic pipe used extensively in Canadian residential construction from the mid-1970s through the late 1990s. It was marketed as a cheaper, easier-to-install alternative to copper and was used for both main water supply lines and branch runs to fixtures. At its peak, Poly-B was installed in an estimated 3 million Canadian homes.

The pipe itself is typically marked with "PB2110" or "Polybutylene" and is almost always grey, though it was occasionally produced in black, blue, or white. The fittings are typically copper or brass with crimp rings. The system is most commonly found in homes built between 1978 and 1998.

Why Poly-B Is a Problem

Poly-B fails in two distinct ways, both expensive and both not covered by standard home insurance in BC:

1. Oxidative Degradation (Most Common)

When Poly-B pipe is exposed to hot water — either from a water heater or from prolonged solar heating of outdoor runs — the pipe's inner walls oxidize. The oxidization process makes the pipe brittle and creates micro-fractures in the polymer chain. Over 10-25 years, this degradation weakens the pipe until it can no longer hold pressure. This is why Poly-B failures almost always manifest as sudden pipe bursts rather than slow leaks: the pipe does not gradually thin, it simply reaches a point where it can no longer contain water pressure and splits.

The reaction is accelerated by:

  • Consistently hot water temperatures (above 60C / 140F)
  • High chlorine content in municipal water supplies
  • Exposure to direct sunlight on outdoor runs
  • Improper installation that left kinks or sharp bends in the pipe

2. Fitting Failure (Equally Serious)

The copper and brass fittings used with Poly-B are subject to a separate failure mode: the metal fittings corrode when in contact with the Poly-B pipe, particularly when the system carries hot water. This corrosion causes the fitting to seize, crack, or develop pinhole leaks. Unlike the pipe itself, fitting failures are harder to predict because they often occur at joints that were already installed incorrectly — a common problem because Poly-B crimp fittings require a specific tool and training that many installers did not receive in the 1980s and 1990s.

How to Tell If You Have Poly-B

The fastest identification is visual. Poly-B pipe is almost always grey, flexible, and typically marked with "PB2110" printed on the outer surface at regular intervals. It is usually found:

  • Ran exposed along basement ceiling joists or in mechanical rooms
  • Coming out of the main water shutoff valve
  • Running to the hot water tank
  • At fixture connection points under sinks and around bathrooms

Some Vancouver homes, particularly in Richmond and East Vancouver, were built with Poly-B running underground from the city water main to the home's main shutoff. This underground section is the hardest to inspect and often the first to fail.

What Poly-B Failure Looks Like

Homeowners typically discover they have a Poly-B problem in one of three ways:

  • Sudden pipe burst: A section of pipe fails under pressure and releases water rapidly. In a basement this can cause $15,000-$75,000 in damage depending on how quickly the main shutoff is reached. Reno Stars has responded to three emergency calls where a Poly-B burst was the trigger event.
  • Slow leak at a fitting: A fitting develops a pinhole leak that produces visible water staining on drywall, warped flooring, or a persistent musty odour. These leaks are often misdiagnosed as roof or exterior leaking for months before the true source is identified.
  • Home inspection before purchase: A pre-purchase home inspection identifies Poly-B as a noted deficiency. This is increasingly common in the Vancouver market as realtors and home inspectors become more educated about Poly-B.

Poly-B and Home Insurance in BC

This is the most urgent financial risk. Several major Canadian insurers — including Aviva, Wawanesa, and Canadian Direct — have issued formal policy exclusions for Poly-B plumbing systems. A home with Poly-B may:

  • Be declined for standard home insurance at renewal
  • Be offered insurance only with aPoly-B exclusion rider, leaving the homeowner fully liable for any water damage
  • Face a significantly higher premium (15-40% surcharge) compared to a home with copper or PEX re-piping
  • Be required to sign a statutory declaration confirming the presence of Poly-B, which creates legal liability if a claim later reveals the insurer was not disclosed

If you have Poly-B and are planning a renovation, most plumbing contractors and financial advisors recommend treating the re-pipe as a prerequisite — the cost of the replacement is almost always less than the cost of a denied insurance claim on a water-damaged home.

Poly-B Replacement Options

Option 1: Full Re-Pipe with PEX (Recommended)

Cross-linked polyethylene (PEX) is the modern standard for residential water supply in Canada. PEX is flexible, freeze-resistant, and carries a manufacturer warranty of 25 years or more. A full re-pipe replaces all Poly-B pipe and fittings with PEX, typically running new lines from the water main entry point to every fixture in the house.

Cost: $8,000-$22,000 depending on home size and complexity

Timeline: 3-7 days for a typical Vancouver detached home

Disruption: Water will be off during working hours; a temporary bypass can maintain toilet access

Permit: A plumbing permit from the City of Vancouver (or relevant municipality) is required for a full re-pipe. Cost: $250-$400 depending on the municipality.

Option 2: Partial Re-Pipe to Affected Sections

If a plumber's inspection confirms that only certain sections of the home are affected — for example, the hot water lines but not the cold water lines — a partial replacement may be appropriate. This is less expensive but leaves some Poly-B in the system, which will eventually need replacement.

Cost: $3,500-$9,000 depending on scope

When appropriate: Very early-stage degradation, where a plumber can confirm the pipe is still in acceptable condition in unaffected sections

Risk: A partial re-pipe that leaves Poly-B in the walls may still trigger insurance concerns, as an insurer's inspector could still flag the remaining system

Option 3: Re-Pipe with Copper

Copper is the traditional choice and carries the longest track record. It is more expensive than PEX and requires more skilled tradespeople to install correctly. Copper is preferred in some heritage contexts or where local building officials are skeptical of PEX (though Vancouver building codes fully accept PEX).

Cost: $14,000-$35,000 for a full copper re-pipe in a Vancouver home

Timeline: 7-14 days

Note: Copper prices fluctuate significantly with commodity markets — get a firm quote before committing

Poly-B Replacement During a Renovation

If you are already planning a renovation, the plumbing work for a Poly-B re-pipe and the renovation can often be coordinated to reduce total cost and disruption. Reno Stars has completed four renovation projects where we replaced the Poly-B system as part of a larger basement renovation or whole-house renovation:

  • The walls were already being opened for the renovation, so the plumber did not need to open them specifically for the re-pipe — saving $2,000-$5,000 in wall repair costs
  • The permit for the plumbing work could be combined with the renovation building permit
  • The timeline added approximately 3-5 days to the overall renovation schedule

If you are considering a renovation and know or suspect you have Poly-B, bring this up at the initial consultation — it is significantly easier to address before walls are closed and flooring is installed.

Vancouver-Specific Considerations

Several factors make Poly-B replacement particularly important in the Vancouver context:

Richmond and Delta Soil Chemistry

Parts of Richmond and Delta have slightly elevated chlorine levels in the municipal water supply due to the delta's tidal influence on water retention. Higher chlorine accelerates Poly-B oxidative degradation, meaning Richmond homes with Poly-B tend to show earlier failure symptoms than equivalent homes in other municipalities.

East Vancouver Basement Suites

East Vancouver has a high concentration of 1970s-1980s basement suite properties with Poly-B. The presence of a secondary suite complicates a re-pipe because the plumber must coordinate work in both the main suite and the basement suite, and may need to provide temporary plumbing for one unit while working in the other. Reno Stars has managed three basement suite re-pipe projects in East Vancouver.

Vancouver Building Permit Requirements

The City of Vancouver requires a plumbing permit for any work that alters the water supply system. A Poly-B re-pipe in Vancouver requires:

  • City of Vancouver plumbing permit ($300 for a full re-pipe)
  • A registered plumber licensed with the City of Vancouver
  • Inspection at rough-in and final stages
  • For properties in a Strata: Strata council approval before work begins (allow 4-6 weeks for the approval process)

For work in other municipalities — Richmond, Burnaby, Surrey, Coquitlam — permit requirements and fees vary. Reno Stars manages the permit application process in all Metro Vancouver municipalities as part of our project management service.

What Poly-B Replacement Actually Costs in Vancouver (2026)

Costs below reflect actual Reno Stars projects in Metro Vancouver, updated for current material and labour conditions:

  • Full PEX re-pipe, 1988 Richmond townhouse (1,400 sq ft): $9,200 — partial scope, replaced hot and cold supply lines in basement and upper floor, fittings at 14 fixture connections
  • Full PEX re-pipe, 1991 Richmond detached home (2,200 sq ft): $14,500 — full re-pipe including underground main line entry section
  • Full PEX re-pipe, 1985 East Vancouver house (1,800 sq ft, basement suite): $18,300 — full re-pipe both units, coordinated with basement renovation
  • Partial re-pipe (hot water lines only), 1992 Coquitlam townhouse: $6,800 — plumber confirmed cold water lines were still in acceptable condition at time of work
  • Emergency repair + full re-pipe, 1989 Surrey house: $21,000 — burst pipe emergency call + full PEX replacement completed as a single project

How to Get Started

Reno Stars offers free Poly-B assessments as part of our initial renovation consultations. We will visually inspect accessible piping, identify the type of fittings used, and provide a written cost estimate for a full or partial re-pipe. If you are planning a renovation, we will include the re-pipe scope in the overall project scope and coordinate with our licensed plumber.

For emergency situations — an active leak or burst — call our office directly. We maintain a relationship with a 24-hour emergency plumber in Metro Vancouver and can often have someone on site within 2 hours during business hours.
contentZh:
如果您拥有的温哥华地区房屋建于1975年至2000年之间，那么您的房屋有大约40%的概率安装了Poly-B管道——一种灰色塑料管道系统，在被明确认定会导致过早故障、集体诉讼和保险拒赔之前，已在数百万加拿大住宅中使用。Reno Stars自2022年以来已在卑诗省大温地区完成了七个Poly-B更换项目，范围从高贵林联排别墅的部分管道更换到1991年列治文独立住宅的全面管道更换。

什么是Poly-B管道

聚丁烯（Poly-B）是一种柔性灰色塑料管，于1970年代中期至1990年代末期在加拿大住宅建筑中广泛使用。它被宣传为铜管的更便宜、更易于安装的替代品，用于主供水管道和固定装置分支管道。在其鼎盛时期，Poly-B被安装在约300万加拿大房屋中。

为什么Poly-B是个问题

Poly-B以两种不同方式出现故障——两种都价格昂贵，在卑诗省都不在标准房屋保险覆盖范围内：

1. 氧化降解（最常见）

当Poly-B管道暴露于热水时——无论是来自热水器还是长时间阳光照射的室外管道——管道内壁会氧化。氧化过程使管道变脆，并在聚合物链中产生微裂纹。在10-25年内，这种降解会削弱管道，直到它无法承受压力。这就是为什么Poly-B故障几乎总是表现为突然的管道爆裂而不是缓慢泄漏：管道不会逐渐变薄，只是在无法再承受水压时裂开。

2. 接头故障（同样严重）

与Poly-B一起使用的铜和黄铜接头会受到另一种故障模式的影响：当系统携带热水时，金属接头会腐蚀。这种腐蚀导致接头卡住、破裂或产生针孔泄漏。与管道本身不同，接头故障更难预测，因为它们通常发生在已经安装不当的接头处——这是一个常见问题，因为Poly-B压接接头需要专门的工具和培训，而许多安装人员在1980年代和1990年代并未接受过相关培训。

如何判断您是否有Poly-B

最快的识别方法是目视检查。Poly-B管道几乎总是灰色、柔韧的，通常标有"PB2110"或"Polybutylene"。它通常出现在：

  • 沿着地下室天花板托梁或机械室暴露安装
  • 从主进水阀伸出
  • 通向热水器的管道
  • 在水槽下方和浴室周围的固定装置连接处

卑诗省的Poly-B和房屋保险

这是最紧迫的财务风险。几家大型加拿大保险公司——包括Aviva、Wawanesa和Canadian Direct——已对Poly-B管道系统发出正式保单排除条款。拥有Poly-B的房屋可能：

  • 续保时被标准房屋保险拒绝
  • 只有携带Poly-B排除条款的保险才能投保，使房主自行承担任何水灾损失的全部责任
  • 面临显著更高的保费（比有铜管或PEX重新布线的房屋高出15-40%）

如果您有Poly-B并计划装修，大多数水管工和财务顾问建议将重新布线作为先决条件——更换的成本几乎总是低于因水灾损失而被拒绝理赔的房屋成本。

Poly-B更换选项

选项1：使用PEX进行全面重新布线（推荐）

交联聚乙烯（PEX）是加拿大住宅供水的现代标准。PEX柔韧、抗冻，且有至少25年的制造商保修。全面重新布线用PEX更换所有Poly-B管道和接头，通常从供水入口点到房屋每个固定装置铺设新管道。

费用：$8,000-$22,000，取决于房屋大小和复杂程度

时间线：典型温哥华独立住宅3-7天

许可证：需要温哥华市（或相关市政当局）的管道许可证。费用：$250-$400。

选项2：部分重新布线至受影响部分

如果水管工的检查确认只有某些部分受影响——例如热水管线但不是冷水管线——部分更换可能更合适。这费用较低，但管道中仍留有一些Poly-B，最终需要更换。

费用：$3,500-$9,000，取决于工程范围

风险：保留Poly-B的部分重新布线仍可能引发保险问题，因为保险检查员可能仍会标记剩余系统

温哥华特定的Poly-B更换费用（2026年）

以下费用反映Reno Stars在大温哥华地区的实际项目，按当前材料和人工条件更新：

  • 1988年列治文联排别墅（1,400平方英尺）全面PEX重新布线：$9,200
  • 1991年列治文独立住宅（2,200平方英尺）全面PEX重新布线：$14,500
  • 1985年东温哥华房屋（1,800平方英尺，带地下室套房）全面PEX重新布线：$18,300
  • 1992年高贵林联排别墅部分重新布线（仅热水管线）：$6,800
  • 1989年素里房屋紧急维修+全面重新布线：$21,000

如何开始

Reno Stars在初始装修咨询中提供免费的Poly-B评估。我们将目视检查可接近的管道，识别所用接头的类型，并提供全面或部分重新布线的书面成本估算。如果您正在计划装修，我们会把重新布线纳入整体项目范围，并与我们的持牌水管工协调。
